examples.facts: On 1 March, Karim Traders sells 100 units on credit at Rs. 1,000 per unit. Unit cost is Rs. 600. Goods are delivered the same day. No discounts or returns expected.
examples.solution: A contract exists and control transfers on delivery, so both performance (delivery) and price (Rs. 100,000) are fixed on 1 March. Recognise revenue of Rs. 100,000 and cost of sales of Rs. 60,000; gross profit Rs. 40,000.
examples.title: Credit sale of goods — revenue and cost recognised on delivery

examples.facts: Year-end inventory: 500 units at cost Rs. 200 each (Rs. 100,000). Estimated selling price Rs. 190 per unit; estimated selling costs Rs. 10 per unit.
examples.solution: NRV per unit = 190 − 10 = Rs. 180, below cost of Rs. 200. Write down by Rs. 20 × 500 = Rs. 10,000 to Rs. 90,000. The write-down is an expense of the period.
examples.title: Inventory write-down to NRV

examples.facts: Machine purchased 1 July for Rs. 1,200,000 (including Rs. 100,000 installation). Useful life 10 years, residual value Rs. 200,000, straight-line. Year-end 31 December.
examples.solution: Depreciable amount = 1,200,000 − 200,000 = Rs. 1,000,000; annual charge Rs. 100,000. Six months to year-end gives Rs. 50,000 depreciation and a carrying amount of Rs. 1,150,000.
examples.title: Machine purchase and part-year depreciation

examples.facts: On 1 January, a company enters a 3-year lease: annual payments of Rs. 120,000 in arrears. Incremental borrowing rate 10%. No initial direct costs or incentives.
examples.solution: Liability = 120,000 × 2.48685 (3-yr annuity at 10%) = Rs. 298,422. Year 1: depreciation Rs. 99,474, interest Rs. 29,842, total expense Rs. 129,316 vs Rs. 120,000 cash paid — the front-loaded profile of IFRS 16.
examples.title: Three-year lease — initial recognition and year 1

examples.facts: A lawsuit for Rs. 500,000 was filed against the company before year-end. Legal advice: it is probable the company will lose and pay around Rs. 300,000.
examples.solution: All three criteria are met: present obligation (past event — the acts leading to the lawsuit), probable outflow, reliable estimate (Rs. 300,000). Recognise a provision; disclose the nature and uncertainties. If the outflow were only possible, disclose a contingent liability instead.
examples.title: Lawsuit provision — all three criteria met

examples.facts: Company buys Rs. 1,000,000 of 5-year government bonds, intending to hold them to collect the contractual interest and principal. Cash flows are fixed interest plus principal (SPPI).

journals.narration: Purchase of bonds (hold to collect, SPPI)
Annual coupon at 5% (simplified; EIR in practice)

examples.solution: Business model is 'hold to collect' and cash flows are SPPI, so the bonds are measured at amortised cost. Interest is recognised by the effective interest method and an expected credit loss allowance is recognised.
examples.title: Bond held to collect — amortised cost

examples.facts: A machine: cost Rs. 800,000, accumulated depreciation Rs. 300,000 (carrying amount Rs. 500,000). Fair value less costs of disposal Rs. 420,000; value in use Rs. 460,000.
examples.solution: Recoverable amount = higher of 420,000 and 460,000 = Rs. 460,000. Carrying amount 500,000 exceeds it by Rs. 40,000 — recognise an impairment loss of Rs. 40,000 in profit or loss. Future depreciation is based on Rs. 460,000.
examples.title: Impairment — recoverable amount is the higher of the two

examples.facts: Accounting depreciation Rs. 200,000; tax depreciation Rs. 350,000. Tax rate 30%. No other differences. (Simplified: the extra Rs. 150,000 tax depreciation creates a taxable temporary difference.)
examples.solution: Tax base of the asset is lower than its carrying amount by Rs. 150,000 — a taxable temporary difference, because less tax will be deductible in future. Recognise a deferred tax liability of Rs. 45,000 (150,000 × 30%).
examples.title: Deferred tax liability from accelerated tax depreciation
